The Fat Cantor Set

What if we dig out less? Removing only length 4−n4^{-n}4−n per interval leaves a set that is compact, nowhere dense and perfect — yet keeps total length 12\frac1221​. Measure and topological size are independent notions.

Examples & Exercises

Consider the fat Cantor set: at stage nnn, from each of the 2n−12^{n-1}2n−1 surviving closed intervals remove the middle open interval of absolute length 4−n4^{-n}4−n. Prove the total removed length over all stages is 12\tfrac1221​ via a geometric series, and check that the length remaining after NNN stages is 1+2−N2\dfrac{1 + 2^{-N}}{2}21+2−N​.

Show proof
  1. At stage nnn there are 2n−12^{n-1}2n−1 surviving closed intervals from stage n−1n-1n−1, and exactly one middle open interval of length 4−n4^{-n}4−n is removed from each. Removed open intervals from different stages and different parent intervals are all pairwise disjoint (each is carved out of the interior of a closed interval, and the surviving sets are nested). So the total length removed through stage NNN is the sum of the per-stage contributions.
  2. The stage-nnn contribution is 2n−1⋅4−n2^{n-1} \cdot 4^{-n}2n−1⋅4−n. Simplifying the exponent, 2n−14n=2n−122n=2−n−1\dfrac{2^{n-1}}{4^n} = \dfrac{2^{n-1}}{2^{2n}} = 2^{-n-1}4n2n−1​=22n2n−1​=2−n−1, so the total removed length is the geometric series ∑n=1∞2−n−1\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} 2^{-n-1}∑n=1∞​2−n−1 with ratio 12\tfrac1221​. Its first term is 14\tfrac1441​, giving 1/41−1/2=12\dfrac{1/4}{1 - 1/2} = \tfrac121−1/21/4​=21​.
  3. The finite-stage version: through stage NNN the total removed is the partial sum ∑n=1N2−n−1=14⋅1−2−N1−1/2=12(1−2−N)\sum_{n=1}^{N} 2^{-n-1} = \tfrac14 \cdot \dfrac{1 - 2^{-N}}{1 - 1/2} = \tfrac12(1 - 2^{-N})∑n=1N​2−n−1=41​⋅1−1/21−2−N​=21​(1−2−N). Starting from [0,1][0,1][0,1], the length remaining after NNN stages is 1−12(1−2−N)=12(1+2−N)1 - \tfrac12(1 - 2^{-N}) = \tfrac12(1 + 2^{-N})1−21​(1−2−N)=21​(1+2−N), tending to 12\tfrac1221​ as N→∞N \to \inftyN→∞. For N=1N = 1N=1 this is 1−14=34=12(1+12)1 - \tfrac14 = \tfrac34 = \tfrac12(1 + \tfrac12)1−41​=43​=21​(1+21​) — the surviving intervals [ 0,38 ][\,0, \tfrac38\,][0,83​] and [ 58,1 ][\,\tfrac58, 1\,][85​,1] with the middle (38,58)(\tfrac38, \tfrac58)(83​,85​) carved out, exactly as the scene shows.
  4. Hence the pairwise-disjoint union GGG of the removed open intervals has Lebesgue measure m(G)=12m(G) = \tfrac12m(G)=21​, and since C=[0,1]∖GC = [0,1] \setminus GC=[0,1]∖G, we get m(C)=1−12=12>0m(C) = 1 - \tfrac12 = \tfrac12 > 0m(C)=1−21​=21​>0. This is where the fat Cantor set parts company with the standard Cantor set (middle third removed each stage, remaining length (2/3)n→0(2/3)^n \to 0(2/3)n→0).

Then δ=∣I∣≤∣J∣=ℓn<δ\delta = \lvert I \rvert \le \lvert J \rvert = \ell_n < \deltaδ=∣I∣≤∣J∣=ℓn​<δ — contradiction.

At stage n+1n+1n+1, JnJ_nJn​ splits into two closed children J′,J′′J', J''J′,J′′ separated by the removed open middle, and xxx belongs to one of them, say J′J'J′. Let U=[0,1]∖CU = [0,1] \setminus CU=[0,1]∖C be the complement of the fat Cantor set. Prove UUU is (relatively) open, dense in [0,1][0,1][0,1], and has m(U)=12m(U) = \tfrac12m(U)=21​. Then finish by completing this table: "empty interior, yet half the length" — measure and topological size are independent notions.

U=⋃stages(removed open intervals)U = \bigcup_{\text{stages}} \text{(removed open intervals)}U=stages⋃​(removed open intervals)
m(U)=12,m(C)=12m(U) = \tfrac12,\quad m(C) = \tfrac12m(U)=21​,m(C)=21​
m=0m>0nowhere densestandard Cantorfat CantordenseQ∩[0,1]irrationals in [0,1]\begin{array}{c|cc} & m = 0 & m > 0 \\ \hline \text{nowhere dense} & \text{standard Cantor} & \textbf{fat Cantor} \\ \text{dense} & \mathbb{Q} \cap [0,1] & \text{irrationals in } [0,1] \end{array}nowhere densedense​m=0standard CantorQ∩[0,1]​m>0fat Cantorirrationals in [0,1]​​
Show proof
  1. UUU is the complement of the closed set CCC, hence relatively open in [0,1][0,1][0,1]. Concretely, UUU is the union of the removed open intervals over all stages — a countable union of pairwise-disjoint open intervals.
  2. Dense: the previous problem showed that every nonempty open interval meets a removed open interval. Hence every open interval contains a point of UUU, so UUU is dense in [0,1][0,1][0,1].
  3. Measure: the removed open intervals are pairwise disjoint, so m(U)=∑n=1∞2n−14−n=12m(U) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} 2^{n-1} 4^{-n} = \tfrac12m(U)=∑n=1∞​2n−14−n=21​ (the geometric series from the first problem). Hence m(C)=m([0,1])−m(U)=1−12=12m(C) = m([0,1]) - m(U) = 1 - \tfrac12 = \tfrac12m(C)=m([0,1])−m(U)=1−21​=21​.
  4. To summarize: CCC is closed, has empty interior (nowhere dense), is perfect, and has length 12\tfrac1221​; its complement UUU is open, dense, and has length 12\tfrac1221​. The table above fills all four cells — the standard Cantor set (nowhere dense, measure 0), the fat Cantor set (nowhere dense, measure 12\tfrac1221​), the rationals in [0,1][0,1][0,1] (dense, measure 0), the irrationals (dense, measure 1). There are even sets that are open and dense with arbitrarily small measure (around each rational qkq_kqk​ take an open interval of radius ε/2k\varepsilon/2^kε/2k: total measure ≤2ε\le 2\varepsilon≤2ε). The punchline: the topological statement "has empty interior" and the measure-theoretic statement "has such-and-such length" impose nothing on each other — and the fat Cantor set is the most dramatic witness to their independence.
